text:
Here are two groups of forty people, and group B scores more than three and a half points higher. So is B better? Here's the catch. Both groups came from the SAME process. There's no real difference at all. So draw both groups again... and this time, A comes out ahead, by one point seven. Again, and again. By about two, then three, then one. Five draws, and the gap is never zero. Randomness makes differences for free. So before you believe any gap, ask one question... could this just be luck?

Noise makes trends, too. Here are two years of a monthly metric. Over the last six months, it fell almost twelve points. Something must have happened... right? Nothing did. Every month is a hundred, plus random noise. The trend was never there. Behind every dataset is a process like this one. Customers deciding, machines running, demand rising and falling. You never see the process itself. You only see what comes out of it... signal, plus noise. The signal is the stable part, here that flat hundred. The noise is everything that wobbles around it. Statistics is how you find the signal through the noise. And the numbers you get are only ever a slice... of something much bigger.

Say you survey five hundred of your three hundred thousand customers. That tells you exactly what those five hundred said. But your question is about all three hundred thousand. Everyone you care about is the population. The part you saw is the sample... here, one customer in six hundred. And often, the population isn't even a list. It's every checkout a design will ever see, and most of them haven't happened yet.

A number that describes the population is a parameter. It's fixed... but you can't see it. A number you compute from the sample is a statistic. You can see it, but it moves. Parameters get Greek letters, like mu for a mean. Statistics get Latin ones, like x-bar. In code, we can cheat and know the truth. Build a population with a mean of a hundred, and sample fifty. Their average is a hundred and one point four. Close, but not on it. That miss isn't a mistake. It's the price of seeing only part.

Now draw fifty more, and fifty more. Twenty samples give twenty different answers. The parameter never moved. Only the statistic did. That makes a statistic a random variable, with a center and a spread of its own. So think in distributions, not points. Any one average is a single draw from that spread. But before you summarize a sample at all... you need to know what KIND of number you're holding.

Take a survey that stores favorite ice cream flavors as numbers. One is vanilla, two is chocolate, three is strawberry. Ten people answer. Average the column, and you get one point eight. There is no flavor one point eight. The math ran fine... but those numbers were labels, not quantities. The honest summary is the most common answer. Vanilla.

So every column is one of two kinds. Categorical data says which group. Numerical data says how much, or how many. Labels split again. Nominal ones have no order, like countries. Ordinal ones do, like shirt sizes, but the gaps between them can be uneven. Numbers split into counts, like logins, and measurements, like price.

The dangerous columns look numerical, but aren't. Take four zip codes. pandas stores them as integers, and averages them without a word. Forty-eight thousand, seven hundred and fifty-five. That isn't a place. It's the average of four labels. One test catches it. Would doubling the value mean anything? Double a price, and it costs twice as much. Double a zip code... and you get nonsense. The data type only says how a number is stored. What it means is your call.

And that call decides what you're allowed to do. Labels get counts and the most common value. Ranks get a median. Quantities get a mean. Later, it picks the test, too. Two categorical columns call for a chi-square test. A number compared across two groups, a t-test. And even a real quantity can mislead. Is its average the typical value? Not always... skew can pull it off center.
